# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: disc-numbers
#| include: false

d_inc_win <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "S1/K0", "win")
d_mkt_win <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "S4/K0", "win")
d_inc_ew5 <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "S1/K0", "eachway")
d_win <- p6_con(p6_test_contrasts, "win", "incumbent")
d_plc <- p6_con(p6_test_contrasts, "place", "incumbent")
dv_win <- p6_valinc(p6_val_incumbent, "win")
```

## What this paper found

The betting rule was not the binding constraint either.

Paper 3 concluded that the linear predictor was not what limited the series,
because a tree ensemble tied it. Paper 5 found that the feature encoding was
worth something on ranking and nothing on ROI. This paper adds the third: the
selection and staking rule was not it. Nine selection rules and three staking
rules, searched out of sample, produced three declarations and all three were
the rule the series already had.

That is a mildly surprising positive for Owen's rule. It is inherited from a
different dataset and its thresholds sit at odd places in this one, and the
obvious criticism of it — that a high model-to-market ratio selects for races
where the model is wrong, which is what paper 4 implies — did not survive
contact with the data. Of the three middle-band rules built to test that
criticism, the two narrowest are last and second-last in every validation
table and the widest is middling. Inverting the filter made things worse.

What it is not is evidence that Owen's rule is good. Against a rule with no
model in it, the win-market difference is
`r p6_fmt_pts(d_win$diff_point)` points on
`r p6_fmt_pts_ci(d_win$ci_lo, d_win$ci_hi)`, and the point estimate favours
the model-free rule. On three of four settlement columns the two cannot be
told apart. The model's contribution to bet selection remains invisible on
this data — the same answer paper 4 reached from a different direction.

## What it did not find

It did not find that the model is worthless. Papers 2b, 3 and 5 measured
ranking, and there the encoder is distinguishably better than every earlier
arm in the series, on nine contrasts with nine intervals excluding zero. A
model can rank better and still not turn that into a bet, because the bet has
to beat a price and the price already contains most of what the ranking
knows.

It did not find that the place result means the model works. The incumbent
beats the control there by `r p6_fmt_pts(d_plc$diff_point)` points on an
interval excluding zero, and that is the only such interval in the paper. It
is a statement about a synthetic place market that prices favourites hardest
(@sec-control), not about model skill.

It did not find that variable staking is a bad idea. It found that staking
proportional to a disagreement is not worth doing when the disagreement
carries no information against the settled price, which is a narrower claim
and one paper 4 already implied.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

**The validation slice is small for a betting question.** It holds
`r p6_comma(n_val_races)` races, and under the incumbent's filter that is
`r p6_comma(dv_win$n_bets)` bets. The incumbent's own win ROI there is
`r p6_fmt_pct(dv_win$roi)` with a 90% interval of
`r p6_fmt_pct_ci(dv_win$ci_lo, dv_win$ci_hi)` — about
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (dv_win$ci_hi - dv_win$ci_lo))` points wide. **The
design cannot see a difference of a few points.** What it can see is a rule
that is badly wrong, or one that bets so rarely the question does not arise;
what it cannot see is the size of edge that would matter commercially. The
declaration should be read as "nothing separated itself from the incumbent",
not as "the incumbent is best". Those are different claims and only the first
is supported.

The same figure bounds the other direction. The incumbent returned
`r p6_fmt_pct(dv_win$roi)` on validation and `r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_win$roi)` on
test, both out of sample, a swing of about twenty points between two
non-overlapping periods. That is what noise looks like at this scale.

**The model was selected with knowledge of the test races.** The betting rule
was not — it was declared and committed before any test target existed — but
five papers of model development have looked at this test split, and the
encoder scoring it here is the one those five papers arrived at. The model
side of every number in this paper carries that history. Only the
betting-rule side is clean.

**The validation slice is not virgin data either.** Paper 5 used it to select
the encoder's architecture, hyperparameters and epoch count. It was not used
for betting rules, and no betting quantity entered any paper-5 decision, so
the search here is not re-using its own selection criterion. But a slice that
has already chosen a model is not the same as an untouched hold-out, and a
rule that happens to suit the architecture that slice selected would not be
caught by this design.

**The test split has one arm on it.** Because the declaration returned the
incumbent, the test contact is two rules, one of which is the comparator.
There was no opportunity for a declared alternative to fail on test, which
means this paper offers no evidence about how well a validation-slice
declaration generalises. A design that declared something other than the
incumbent would have produced that evidence; this one did not get the chance.

**Every arm loses money.** Stated without qualification: on the test split,
at real starting prices, neither rule returns a profit on any market.

## Break-even, and what would settle it {#sec-breakeven}

The margin decomposition (@sec-margin) puts a number on the gap. The
incumbent loses `r p6_fmt_pct(-d_inc_win$roi)` on the win market at the
starting price and returns `r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_win$roi_fair)` at a book with
the over-round taken out. Its each-way return under paper 5's terms is
`r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_ew5$roi)`, the closest any arm in the series has come to
break-even. So the question is not whether the model is a long way from
profitable — it is whether it is roughly one bookmaker's margin away.

The direction that would answer it is prices better than the starting price.
The starting price is the settled price, after the market has absorbed
everything it is going to absorb. Paper 4 found the model adds nothing
against it, but adds substantially against the pre-race racecard forecast
published the night before. If a price closer to the forecast than to the
settled price were available at bet time — an exchange price early in the
market, before liquidity builds — the same selection could face a materially
smaller margin, and possibly a positive one.

**This dataset cannot settle that.** Smartform holds the overnight forecast
price and the settled starting price, and nothing in between. There is no
exchange price history: no series of prices from market open to the off, no
record of what was actually available at any moment, and no depth alongside
it. A rule that looks break-even against a hypothetical fair book is not
evidence that a real counterparty would have taken the bet at that price, in
that size.

What it would take is exchange price and volume history for these races,
timestamped, and a repeat of this design against prices taken at a declared
time before the off rather than at the off. Until that exists, the honest
statement is the one the numbers support: the model does not beat the settled
market, the rule that bets it is the best of the nine tried and is
indistinguishable from backing the favourite, the gap on the best market
tested is about the size of the over-round, and whether an earlier price
closes that gap is untested.
